title: The Lighthouse Ledger
scenes: Scene 1. The island of Skerholm, November. Anselm Brandt, keeper of the lighthouse for thirty-one years, is found at the foot of the spiral stairs at half past nine in the morning by his wife Marta. His neck is broken. The lamp above is still burning, which it should not be after dawn. Marta tells the constable that Anselm went up to the lamp room at six as he did every day, and that she heard nothing. The island has no police of its own; Captain Reyes of the coast guard cutter takes charge until the mainland sends someone.

Scene 2. Dr. Ilse Varga, the island's physician, examines the body in the lamp room at a quarter to eleven. She says Anselm has been dead for about three hours, which puts the fall at around half past seven. Her medical bag sits open on the keeper's desk; the constable, who is counting everything out of habit, notes that the morphine tray holds four vials where the printed label on the tray says six. Dr. Varga says two were used last week on a fisherman's crushed hand and she has not restocked. She signs the preliminary certificate: accidental fall.

Scene 3. Oskar Lind, Anselm's nephew, arrives from the mainland on the noon ferry. He is twenty-six, in debt from a failed boat-repair business, and the only heir after Marta. He says he last spoke to his uncle three weeks ago, by letter, about a loan Anselm refused. The ferryman confirms Oskar boarded on the mainland at ten. Oskar asks twice whether the will is in the house.

Scene 4. Captain Reyes asks everyone where they were between six and nine. Marta: in the kitchen, then the henhouse. Dr. Varga: at home in the village until the constable fetched her at nine, she says, since her first patient was due at half past nine. Tomasz Kowal, the fisherman: on the water from five, back at the harbour at eight. Oskar: on the mainland, as the ferryman says. Reyes himself was aboard the cutter, anchored off the north point, with four crew.

Scene 5. The keeper's ledger is kept in the lamp room: every visit, every delivery, every dose of the morphine Anselm took for his back since the accident two winters ago, in his own careful hand. The last entry, dated the previous Tuesday, records 'Dr. V., two vials, hand of T. Kowal'. The constable finds the page oddly clean compared with the ones before it, but says nothing yet.

Scene 6. Tomasz Kowal mends nets on the quay and talks freely. His hand is bandaged; he says the doctor set it ten days ago and gave him 'something for the pain, one injection, that was all'. He also mentions, between other things, that he saw the doctor's green bicycle leaning against the lighthouse wall when he rowed past at about seven that morning, and thought the keeper must be ill again.

Scene 7. Marta, calmer now, shows the constable the household accounts. Anselm's pension was small and the lighthouse is to be automated in the spring; they were to lose the house. She mentions that Anselm had grown 'strange' in the last month, sleeping badly, saying the doctor's injections no longer helped and that he would write to the mainland about it. She does not know what he meant.

Scene 8. The constable returns to the ledger with a glass. The ink of the last entry smears under a wet thumb, while the entries above it, weeks older, do not. The handwriting is a good imitation of Anselm's but the figure 2 is made with a loop Anselm never used. Whoever wrote it had access to the lamp room and to the ledger, and wanted the morphine count to come out right.

Scene 9. Oskar is found in the keeper's study going through the desk. He admits he was looking for the will; he says he owes money to people on the mainland who do not wait. The will, when Marta produces it, leaves everything to her for her lifetime. Oskar did not know this. He is sullen but, as the ferryman's timing stands, he was on the mainland when Anselm fell.

Scene 10. Captain Reyes gathers the facts in the harbour office. Dr. Varga, reading over his notes, corrects the time of death to 'between seven and half past' without being asked, and adds that the keeper's back had been getting worse and that confusion, even a fall, 'is what one expects with his dosage'. Nobody has told her the dosage was in question. The constable notes that the morphine tray label said six and that Kowal remembers one injection, not two.

Scene 11. A letter is found in the keeper's coat, unposted, addressed to the harbour medical board on the mainland. Anselm writes that the doctor has been recording doses he never received, that he believes she is taking the morphine herself, and that he intends to show the ledger to the board when the inspector comes in December. The letter is dated the day before he died.

Scene 12. Confronted with the letter, the wet ink and the bicycle, Dr. Ilse Varga admits it. She had been dependent on morphine for a year and covered the missing vials in the keeper's ledger, in his hand, after each visit. When Anselm told her he would write to the board, she came at seven, argued with him on the stairs, and pushed him. She then rewrote the last entry and set her own time of death to cover the hour. She is taken to the mainland on the cutter.
